# BookBuddies CS Team Debrief and Owner Responses

10/28/2026

## Overall comments and key updates

1. I agree with your “diagnosis” that everything the CS Team has designed so far—the recommender, catalog, badges, dashboards, etc.—is primarily a software problem. Once BookBuddies moves toward public release, however, it becomes more than that. It will involve other people’s children, outside vendors, financial transactions, and eventually a handoff from the CS Team. At that point, much of the work involves people (end users, vendors, operators, etc.), policies, and legal/administrative requirements that are beyond the CS Team’s responsibilities.
   - A broader public release is the long-term goal, but the current phase is focused on developing the prototype. The long-term operating and maintaining unit has not yet been finalized. For now, please build with future broader release in mind while treating the current version as a limited prototype.
2. I also agree with your distinction that we are building to the COPPA Rule, but not claiming that BookBuddies is COPPA compliant. Your brief helped me think through several parts of the current design, and I have made some updates that are reflected in my responses below.
   - One important change is how we handle child feedback. I would like to remove free-text notes/reviews from the child side. Children’s responses will be limited to structured choices, such as Yes/Maybe/No, reasons for “Not for Me,” ratings, and other predefined options. Instead, parents can provide optional free-text notes or feedback. This should reduce the chance that children unintentionally enter identifying or sensitive information while still giving BookBuddies useful information for personalization.
     - The parent notes box can be limited to 250 characters and prompted with something like: “Share anything that may help BookBuddies better understand your child’s reading interests and provide more relevant recommendations. Please do not include personal, identifying, sensitive, or confidential information, such as full names, school names, addresses, or contact information.”
3. I made a related change to Step 8 in the PPT flowchart to better reflect how BookBuddies learns: Kid behavior (kid’s choices and ratings) + parent context (parent input and optional free-text notes) + history (longitudinal data tracking kid reading activities included in Bookshelf activity) → BookBuddies learns.
4. I also want to keep the longitudinal aspect of BookBuddies. The system should be able to connect a child’s reading interests, choices, and responses over time using an internal child ID. This supports personalization without requiring the reading data to be tied directly to the child’s name. The same information may also support periodic feedback to children and parents, such as a weekly dashboard showing the child’s reading journey, changing interests, bookshelf activity, and progress.
5. Related to “success metrics,” I added a Weekly Parent Notification to the design. This is a weekly check-in notification to the parent only: “Has [Child Profile Name] finished [Book in Reading Now]? Tap to let them rate it.” After the child rates the book, BookBuddies can immediately provide new recommendations based on the rating. The success definition is in #14.
6. Related to Book Dataset #11, I would like to start with the curated seed catalog rather than Kaggle/GitHub data (see the cataglog in the attachment). The seed will allow us to build and test the catalog structure and initial recommendation logic. However, the catalog should be structured so we can later expand from the small hand-labeled set to thousands of titles, such as through Open Library, without rebuilding the system.

## Overall

Conceptually, the platform is shifting toward a parent-monitored, child-participating model. Parents set up and oversee the account, provide information that may require adult judgment, receive notifications, and have visibility into the child’s reading activity. Children participate directly through age-appropriate, structured interactions such as choosing books, responding to recommendations, managing their Bookshelf, and rating books. This keeps the child actively involved while adding a layer of parental oversight and protection.

Design-wise, for V1, I would like us to build the underlying structure with future growth in mind—particularly a scalable book catalog, longitudinal interaction data, and parent re-engagement/notifications. The goal is not to build all future functionality now, but to avoid design choices that would make these expansions difficult later.
